newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Moldavian airline flies day-old chicks ex-Budapest.
newsitem.headline: Moldavian airline flies day-old chicks ex-Budapest.

text.p: Privately-owned Moldavian Airlines SA said on Friday it planned this year to carry 14 tonnes of day-old chicks on chartered Ilyushin Il-18 'Coot' aircraft from Budapest to the Moldovan capital of Chisinau.
"We will carry day-old chickens on four flights this year with 3.5 tonnes per shipment," the airline's cargo manager Dan Ctratan told Reuters.
"This is a seasonal business that we started last year," Ctratan said. "It lasts from January to May, and it generates three to eight shipments a year. This year we've already done three flights."
Moldavian Airlines also charters flights on leased Il-18s for cargo and passengers once a month to Turkmenbasi in the central Asian state of Turkmenistan, once part of the former Soviet Union.
"A Moldovan company has been exploring for oil there, and we carry about 50 of their employees every month," Ctratan said. "We carry an awful lot of baggage and food for them too."
The airline also leases Il-18s to charter routes once or twice a month to Karachi, the capital of the Sind province of Pakistan, he said.
"We import a lot of general goods from Karachi, mainly household items and clothing," he added. "Moldovan tourists also bring a lot of baggage back from shopping."
Moldavian Airlines also operates two scheduled routes to Russia.

The airline flies its own Tupolev Tu-134 'Crusty' airplane to Moscow on Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays. And it flies leased Yakovlev Yak-40 'Codling' aircraft to Rostov-on-Don on Mondays and Thursdays.

"We take beverages, foodstuff, medical supplies and pharmaceuticals on these routes," Ctratan said. "This business has been increasing. Maybe it's cheaper for Russians to get these goods from us than other countries."
In total cargo trade, Moldavian Airlines imported 26.8 tonnes and exported 9.1 tonnes in 1996. It imported 22.1 tonnes and exported 3.4 tonnes in 1995.
"Imports have prevailed over exports because of Moldova's economic situation -- everything is down," Ctratan said. "But I am sure that our exports will increase, especially to Russia."
The airlines also hoped to start exporting Moldovan wine regularly, he said, noting that it already has shipped samples to Italy via Budapest on its new route to Milan on Wednesdays.

"We have transported maybe 10 to 20 bottles of wine," he added. "If the samples result in regular business, we probably would charter some flights for the wine, but it will be hard because Italy already has its own wine industry."
The route to Milan is part of a group of scheduled flights Moldavian Airlines started on March 30 with a Saab-340 airplane that it bought recently from Swissair AG, he said.
The Saab-340 flies daily from Chisinau to Budapest. It continues to Prague on Thursdays and Sundays and to Verona, Italy, on Mondays and Saturdays.
The routes to Milan and Verona return to Chisinau via Budapest, and the Prague flights return direct to the Moldovan capital, he said.
On Tuesday, the plane makes two trips only to Budapest.
The 33-seat Saab-340 has cargo capacity of 740 kilograms, but most of the storage space is used for passenger baggage, he said.
-- Ryan Tutak, Budapest newsroom (36 1) 327 4040
